title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: What had been, for almost a full year, Vronsky's one consuming desire — replacing every desire he'd had before — and what had been for Anna an impossible, terrifying, and precisely for that reason even more intoxicating dream of happiness — that desire was now fulfilled. He stood before her, pale, his lower jaw trembling, begging her to calm down, without knowing how or why.
"Anna! Anna!" he said, his voice breaking, "Anna, for God's sake!..."

But the louder he spoke, the lower she bent her head — once proud and lighthearted, now overcome with shame — and she slid down from the sofa where she'd been sitting, sinking to the floor at his feet; she would have collapsed onto the carpet if he hadn't caught her.
"My God! Forgive me!" she said, sobbing, pressing his hands against her chest.

She felt so sinful, so guilty, that there was nothing left for her to do but humble herself and beg forgiveness; and since there was no one else left in her life but him, it was to him that she directed her plea. Looking at him, she felt her humiliation almost as a physical thing, and she couldn't say anything more. He felt what a murderer must feel looking at the body he's just taken the life from. That body — the life he'd taken from it — was their love, the first stage of it. There was something horrifying and repulsive in remembering what had been bought at this terrible price of shame. Shame at their bared, naked souls crushed her and spread to him. But despite all the murderer's horror at the sight of his victim's body, he had to cut it up, hide it, make use of what his crime had won him.

And with something like fury, almost like passion — the way a murderer falls on the body and drags and hacks at it — that's how he covered her face and shoulders with kisses. She held his hand and didn't move. "Yes — these kisses, this is what's been bought with this shame. Yes, and this one hand, which will always be mine — the hand of my accomplice." She lifted that hand and kissed it. He dropped to his knees, trying to see her face, but she hid it and said nothing. Finally, as if forcing herself, she stood up and pushed him away. Her face was still beautiful, but only more pitiful for it.
"It's over," she said. "I have nothing left but you. Remember that."
"I could never forget what is now my whole life. For one moment of this happiness..."
"Happiness!" she said, with horror and disgust, and her horror passed into him without her meaning it to. "For pity's sake — not a word, not another word."
She got up quickly and moved away from him.

"Not another word," she repeated, and with a look of cold despair he couldn't understand, she left him. She felt that at that moment she couldn't put into words the shame, the rapture, and the horror of stepping into this new life, and she didn't want to talk about it — didn't want to cheapen the feeling with the wrong words. But later, too — the next day, and the day after that — she still couldn't find the words to capture the tangle of what she felt; she couldn't even find the thoughts to think it through clearly in her own mind.

She told herself: "No, I can't think about it right now — later, when I'm calmer." But that calm never came; every time the thought rose up of what she'd done, of what would happen to her, of what she ought to do, a wave of horror swept over her and she pushed the thoughts away.

But in her dreams, where she had no control over her own thoughts, her situation showed itself to her in its full, ugly nakedness. One dream came to her almost every night. She dreamed that both men were her husbands at once, that both were showering her with affection. Alexey Alexandrovitch was crying, kissing her hands, saying, "How happy we are now!" And Alexey Vronsky was there too, and he was her husband as well. And she marveled that it had ever seemed impossible, explaining to them, laughing, that it was really so much simpler than that, and that now they were all happy and content. But the dream weighed on her like a nightmare, and she'd wake from it in terror.
